summary.title: Git Workflow
summary.one_liner: Learn how a centralized Git workflow works, how to handle push conflicts with rebase, and how it compares to feature branching, Gitflow and forking workflows.
keywords: choose a git workflow for team
takeaways: The Centralized Workflow uses one central bare repository and a single main branch, similar to SVN, and suits small teams migrating from SVN.
Use git pull --rebase before pushing so your commits sit on top of upstream history, avoiding merge commits and keeping history linear.
Git rebase conflicts are resolved commit by commit with git status, git add, and git rebase --continue, or undone with git rebase --abort.
No single Git workflow fits every team; choose based on team culture, scaling, ease of undoing mistakes, and release schedule.
Feature Branching, Gitflow and Forking extend the centralized model with dedicated feature branches, strict release branches, or per-developer server repositories.
summary.summary: The article explains what a Git workflow is and surveys common options for software teams, with the Centralized Workflow as the main walkthrough. It covers creating a bare central repository, cloning, committing locally, pushing to main, and handling rejected pushes by rebasing and resolving conflicts, using a John and Mary example. It then briefly describes Feature Branching, Gitflow (from a 2010 post by Vincent Driessen), and Forking workflows, and closes with guidelines on short-lived branches, easy reverts, and matching release schedules.
